name: OpenCV (5.x DNN engine)
baseline: ONNX Runtime 1.25.1 (official release binaries), CPU inference
workload: CPU inference time in milliseconds for 60+ ONNX models (YOLOv3/v4/v8, ResNet, MobileNetv2, ViT, SAM2 encoder, Fast Neural Style, SFace, CRNN, ...) on five machines (Intel i9, Intel i7, Apple M1, Apple M5, AMD), new OpenCV 5.x DNN engine versus ONNX Runtime 1.25.1.
claimed_speedup: Wiki says the new engine delivers 'competitive CPU inference performance, matching or beating ONNX Runtime on many models'. Examples, ms OpenCV vs ONNX Runtime: AMD VIT_Base_Patch16_224 27.69 vs 55.4, YOLOv4 121.24 vs 338.87, YOLOv8 14.65 vs 21.95, MobileNetv2 2.13 vs 3.48; Intel i9 Fast Neural Style 14.86 vs 40.89, YOLOv4 106.09 vs 179.31; Intel i7 YOLOv4 331.39 vs 794.21; Apple M1 YOLOv4 482.87 vs 1001.12, ResNet_50_v1 27.58 vs 37.19. Not uniformly faster: i9 CRNN 15.56 vs 1.79, RAFT 1193 vs 685.2; i7 ResNet_50_v1 18.51 vs 13.28. Tally of the full tables (derived from page data): OpenCV faster on 24 of 65 models (i9), 19 of 64 (i7), 42 of 63 (M1), 36 of 62 (M5, 2 ties), 54 of 61 (AMD); geometric-mean ONNX Runtime/OpenCV time ratio 0.93 (i9), 0.78 (i7), 1.01 (M1), 1.01 (M5), 1.62 (AMD) (derived from page data, rows with two numeric values only).
hardware: Intel i9, Intel i7, Apple M1, Apple M5 and 'AMD' as labelled on the page; exact CPU models, core counts and thread settings not stated
stars_or_usage: 91.2k stars; de facto standard computer-vision library
tradeoffs: The 5.x DNN engine is new and supports about 64% of the ONNX specification according to the OpenCV 5 wiki page; some models fail ('error' for RAFT on i7 with OpenCV). The DNN module is a small part of a large library; ONNX Runtime can optionally be linked into OpenCV 5 as an alternative engine (WITH_ONNXRUNTIME). Not a training framework.
caveats: First-party wiki page (OpenCV project, edited 2026-06-05). Results are mixed: OpenCV wins on a minority of models on Intel machines (24/65, 19/64) and a majority on Apple and AMD. The geometric means I derived are close to or below 1.0 on Intel, so the headline 'matching or beating' only holds on many, not most, Intel models. No OpenCV build flags or version, no ONNX Runtime thread or execution-provider settings, no exact CPU models, and no benchmark script are given, hence tier C. Baseline is ONNX Runtime, not TensorFlow or PyTorch; I could not open learnopencv.com (blocked here); a search snippet reports an older first-party LearnOpenCV post (DenseNet121 on Colab Xeon CPUs, OpenCV 4.5.1 under 200 ms vs TensorFlow 2.4 near 1 s, PyTorch slightly faster than OpenCV) which I did not verify. Other first-party speed claims on the OpenCV 5 wiki page (https://github.com/opencv/opencv/wiki/OpenCV-5): warpAffine/warpPerspective/remap '10% to over 300%' faster and TRUCO findContours 'several times faster' are against earlier OpenCV 4.x, not an outside baseline. This repo is listed twice in the source list (github.com/opencv and Itseez/opencv, the old home of the same project); both lines folded into this one record.

name: OpenEXR
baseline: TinyEXR v3 (pure-C11 EXR codec, in-tree deflate, PIZ and HTJ2K paths)
workload: Single-threaded, fully in-memory encode and decode of one 660x440 four-channel HALF image (asakusa.exr) per compression codec (none, RLE, ZIP, ZIPS, PIZ, PXR24, B44, HTJ2K), megapixels per second, OpenEXR 4.0-dev versus TinyEXR v3 built dependency-free.
claimed_speedup: From the benchmark doc's TL;DR (rival-authored): on the DEFLATE family and PIZ with TinyEXR's dependency-free codec, 'OpenEXR leads (about 1.2x ZIP, about 1.8x PXR24, about 2.1x ZIPS)' on single-thread decode because of its libdeflate backend; single-thread encode OpenEXR 'about 1.5x on ZIP/ZIPS, about 1.8x on PXR24, and about 3x on HTJ2K'. The README summary says decode PIZ about 2.7x and HTJ2K about 2.5-3x in OpenEXR's favour. Refreshed 2026-08-08 table (TinyEXR default build with libdeflate), MP/s TinyEXR vs OpenEXR: htj2k256 decode 24.1 vs 29.8, htj2k32 decode 23.5 vs 27.9 (OpenEXR 1.2x and 1.19x, derived from page data), piz decode 33.8 vs 35.6. Same doc also says TinyEXR wins or ties elsewhere (none decode 1380 vs 389, rle decode 114 vs 45.5, ZIP decode with libdeflate 80.8 vs 58.8).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 (TinyEXR V3_OPT=-O3; compiler version not stated); OpenEXR 4.0-dev, commit not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16C/32T, Zen2), avx2+f16c, machine idle
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; reference implementation of the EXR format used across film VFX tools
tradeoffs: Heavier than TinyEXR: depends on Imath, a vendored libdeflate, vendored zstd (3.5) and OpenJPH for HTJ2K, with its own internal thread pool. The C core (OpenEXRCore) sits under the C++ API since 3.3.
caveats: Evidence is a rival project's benchmark (TinyEXR author), not an OpenEXR claim, and it is mixed: OpenEXR wins only against TinyEXR's in-tree dependency-free deflate/PIZ/HTJ2K paths; once TinyEXR links the same libdeflate it matches or beats OpenEXR on ZIP/ZIPS/PXR24 and wins 16-thread ZIP/ZIPS decode (339.6 vs 226.6 and 358.5 vs 151.1 MP/s). The per-codec in-tree numbers sit in SVG charts I could not read, so the quoted ratios come from the TL;DR text and the README; the README and the doc disagree on PIZ (README 2.7x for OpenEXR, doc after the PIZ rewrite 33.8 vs 35.6, about 1.05x). The doc's OpenEXR HTJ2K figures are 'the latest available same-machine OpenJPH baseline', not measured in the same run, and the doc's own refreshed table shows TinyEXR faster on HTJ2K encode (18.7 vs 16.4), contradicting the '3x HTJ2K encode' TL;DR line. One small 660x440 image, which limits thread scaling. Tier A is literal (public bench_compare code, CPU model and gcc -O3 stated) but reliability is lower than usual for A. OpenEXR's own release notes (CHANGES.md 3.3, 3.5) give only unquantified or self-relative speed claims (zstd 'slightly faster than ZIPS', htj2k32 4-6x faster than htj2k256, default zip level 4 halves compression time), no outside baseline. I did not open openexr.com.
